title: Questions and answers: price, time, ownership, security | dadmor
description: Straight answers to the twelve questions people ask before starting: how the price is worked out, how long it takes, who owns what, and why we won't guarantee SEO results.

og.title: Questions and answers: price, time, ownership, security | dadmor
og.description: Straight answers to the twelve questions people ask before starting: how the price is worked out, how long it takes, who owns what, and why we won't guarantee SEO results.

acceptedAnswer.text: dadmor is a small, technical studio. We build websites, design interfaces, work out business models, write documentation, run penetration tests and make content for founders and small businesses. We only take a few projects at a time, so the people who write your scope are the people who do the work.

mainEntity.name: How do you work out the price?

acceptedAnswer.text: We don't quote off the top of our heads. First we talk through what you need, then we send a written proposal with a fixed price for a clearly defined piece of work. We've also laid out what a website price is actually made of, hour by hour, in How much does a website cost?
It depends on the size of the job and on whether your content is ready. The proposal includes a schedule, and it's an honest estimate, not a guarantee.

mainEntity.name: What if my content isn't ready yet?

acceptedAnswer.text: That's fine, as long as you tell us at the start. Whether content is ready affects the size of the job, so it goes into the scope in writing.

mainEntity.name: What happens once you hand it over?

acceptedAnswer.text: We walk you through everything and hand over the documentation, so you, or whoever comes next, can keep the work running. How revisions or retests work for your service is written in that service's scope.

mainEntity.name: Who owns the site, the code, the domain and the content?

acceptedAnswer.text: You do. The code, the domain, the hosting account and the content are all handed over in your name, not ours.

mainEntity.name: What is a penetration test, exactly, and what isn't it?

acceptedAnswer.text: A penetration test means a person goes through your system by hand, the way an attacker would, but only within an agreed scope and only with your written permission. We work to PTES and OWASP WSTG, score what we find with CVSS, and report it twice over: a plain executive report and a technical one. One retest is included.

mainEntity.name: Can you guarantee we'll rank on Google?

acceptedAnswer.text: No, and be careful with anyone who does. Nobody can honestly promise a set Google ranking. We can build pages that are structured well, load fast, and ready to be found.

With the project estimator, or just the contact form. The estimator builds you a brief you can print and send us. We've published the actual scope template we sign before starting: What is a project scope? Take dadmor’s real template.

mainEntity.name: What if I change my mind halfway through?

acceptedAnswer.text: It happens. A lot, actually. We write the change down, then decide together what gets added to the scope and what moves out to make room.

mainEntity.name: Can you work alongside our other teams?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, happily. We work with your developers, your designer or your marketing team, and the scope says plainly who is responsible for which part.

mainEntity.name: What happens to my data in your forms and tools?

acceptedAnswer.text: By default, this site collects nothing about you and uses no cookies or trackers. The estimator and the security self-check run entirely in your own browser, and your answers go nowhere.

<button type="button" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-1-en" data-faq-btn="None">What is dadmor?</button>

items: dadmor is a small, technical studio. We build websites, design interfaces, work out business models, write documentation, run penetration tests and make content for founders and small businesses. We only take a few projects at a time, so the people who write your scope are the people who do the work.

blocks.html: <button type="button" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-2-en" data-faq-btn="None">How do you work out the price?</button>

items: We don't quote off the top of our heads. First we talk through what you need, then we send a written proposal with a fixed price for a clearly defined piece of work.

The estimator only shows a size band, S, M or L. It never shows a price. What drives the price is the number of pages or features, any integrations, how ready your content is, and the kind of project. Marketing is the exception in shape only: a fixed monthly amount, still set in the same written proposal.
We've also laid out what a website price is actually made of, hour by hour, in How much does a website cost?

blocks.html: <button type="button" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-3-en" data-faq-btn="None">How long will it take?</button>

items: It depends on the size of the job and on whether your content is ready. The proposal includes a schedule, and it's an honest estimate, not a guarantee.

The usual culprit is content that isn't ready. After that, late feedback, and logins nobody can find. Got a fixed date? Put it in the estimator. It goes into your brief flagged as a risk, so we talk about it from the start.

blocks.html: <button type="button" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-4-en" data-faq-btn="None">What if my content isn't ready yet?</button>

items: That's fine, as long as you tell us at the start. Whether content is ready affects the size of the job, so it goes into the scope in writing.

You've got two options: get the content ready yourself by an agreed date, or add writing to the scope, under Marketing and content. Either way, we sort the structure early, so you know exactly which text is needed, where it goes, and how long it should be.

blocks.html: <button type="button" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-5-en" data-faq-btn="None">What happens once you hand it over?</button>

items: We walk you through everything and hand over the documentation, so you, or whoever comes next, can keep the work running. How revisions or retests work for your service is written in that service's scope.

After the handover period, support only happens under a written agreement. The defaults: for websites and UI/UX, we fix issues you report in the first 14 days after launch; for documentation, one round of revisions within 14 days; for penetration testing, one retest of the findings we reported, within 60 days. That retest is included in the price.

blocks.html: <button type="button" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-6-en" data-faq-btn="None">Who owns the site, the code, the domain and the content?</button>

items: You do. The code, the domain, the hosting account and the content are all handed over in your name, not ours.

The costs are yours too: domain, hosting, any third party services. Accounts are set up in your name from day one, never ours. If we use a library or a font with its own licence, that licence is listed in your handover documents.

blocks.html: <button type="button" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-7-en" data-faq-btn="None">What is a penetration test, exactly, and what isn't it?</button>

items: A penetration test means a person goes through your system by hand, the way an attacker would, but only within an agreed scope and only with your written permission. We work to PTES and OWASP WSTG, score what we find with CVSS, and report it twice over: a plain executive report and a technical one. One retest is included.

It isn't an automated scan. And it doesn't prove your system is "secure": it shows what we found, in that scope, at that time, and what we didn't test. Before any testing we need a written scope, your signed permission, and an NDA. The security self check on this site isn't a penetration test either.

blocks.html: <button type="button" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-8-en" data-faq-btn="None">Can you guarantee we'll rank on Google?</button>

items: No, and be careful with anyone who does. Nobody can honestly promise a set Google ranking. We can build pages that are structured well, load fast, and ready to be found.

In practice that means pages with a proper heading structure, metadata and a sitemap, decent load speed, Persian and English versions with the right language tags, and content that answers what people actually search for. Where you end up ranking also depends on your competitors, on time, and on things neither of us controls.

blocks.html: <button type="button" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-9-en" data-faq-btn="None">So how do we start?</button>

items: With the project estimator, or just the contact form. The estimator builds you a brief you can print and send us.
Then we talk it through, that's the Discover step, and you get a written proposal with the scope, the deliverables and a fixed price. Nothing starts until you've approved that proposal.
We've published the actual scope template we sign before starting: What is a project scope? Take dadmor’s real template.

blocks.html: <button type="button" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-10-en" data-faq-btn="None">What if I change my mind halfway through?</button>

items: It happens. A lot, actually. We write the change down, then decide together what gets added to the scope and what moves out to make room.

If the change makes the job bigger, you get a written addendum first, showing what it does to the cost and the schedule, before we do any of it. Small changes during Design are just normal work. That step exists so you see the direction early.

blocks.html: <button type="button" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-11-en" data-faq-btn="None">Can you work alongside our other teams?</button>

items: Yes, happily. We work with your developers, your designer or your marketing team, and the scope says plainly who is responsible for which part.

We hand things over so another team can pick them up: documented code, design specs, and reports a developer can follow without us in the room. Nobody outside works on your project unless they're named in your scope. If a specialist is needed, their role goes into the scope before work starts.

blocks.html: <button type="button" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-12-en" data-faq-btn="None">What happens to my data in your forms and tools?</button>

items: By default, this site collects nothing about you and uses no cookies or trackers. The estimator and the security self-check run entirely in your own browser, and your answers go nowhere.
The contact form only sends anything when you submit it yourself. The full detail is on the privacy page. Privacy page
